The defect class: a mutating command ships without appending an audit event,\n//! so the live event sequence stops being a sound dirtiness signal. The failure is silent: each command succeeded, and\n25\tnothing in its output says the durable copy moved.\n26\t\n27\tThat is not a hypothetical. The surrounding environment already encodes\n28\t\"flush before you commit\" as an operating rule for agents precisely because\n29\tthe tool does not do it, and a checkpoint restored after a missed flush loses\n30\twhatever the last session did.\n31\t\n32\tThe obvious remedy is the one a neighbouring tool already ships: flush\n33\tautomatically after every successful mutation, and leave `sync flush-only` as\n34\tan idempotent final check. Adopting it here is a change to checkpoint\n35\tsemantics and to the published command contract, so it requires this record.\n36\t\n37\t### What measurement shows\n38\t\n39\tFlush cost was measured against the shipped `bead` 0.1.3 binary in a scratch\n40\tworkspace on the development host:\n41\t\n42\t| Issues | `sync flush-only` wall time | Checkpoint bytes |\n43\t| --- | --- | --- |\n44\t| 100 | 0.01 s | 78 KB |\n45\t| 400 | 0.03 s | 357 KB |\n46\t| 1600 | 0.07 s | 1.47 MB |\n47\t\n48\tFlush is linear in total workspace size, because\n49\t`publish_forensic_checkpoint` re-reads every issue, event, and receipt and\n50\tre-serializes a complete monolith on each call. At 1610 issues a `bead create`\n51\tcosts about 9 ms and a flush about 52 ms, so flushing on every mutation would\n52\tmake each mutation roughly **6.8x** more expensive, with the multiplier\n53\tgrowing linearly as the workspace grows.\n54\t\n55\tWall time is the smaller problem. The monolithic writer instead names the root from the generation\n61\t   ID — `src/service/checkpoint.rs:3567` writes\n62\t   `objects/{generation_id}.jsonl`. The sharded writer does use content\n63\t   hashes, but sharded mode is unreachable: `cmd_sync_flush_only` hardcodes\n64\t   `CheckpointMode::Monolithic`. Two consecutive flushes with byte-identical\n65\t   content were observed to produce two distinct objects (18 → 20). Dedup can\n66\t   never hit.\n67\t2. **Tombstones are declared but never applied.** Section 6.2 step 6 requires\n68\t   applying the pointer-declared tombstones after the pointer commits.\n69\t   `current.json` was observed declaring 18 `deleted_paths`, with all 18 still\n70\t   present on disk — and with `current.json` itself wrongly listed among them.\n71\t   Ten mutate-and-flush cycles at ~1600 issues grew the checkpoint from 3\n72\t   objects / 1.47 MB to 13 objects / 7.83 MB.\n73\t3. **Most mutations do not advance the event sequence.** The dirtiness\n74\t   contract in section 6.2 is \"every committed semantic mutation advances the\n75\t   live event sequence.\" It does not hold. Until every prerequisite in section 6.2.1 of the\n98\tplan passes, the default remains explicit flush, and the automatic path is\n99\tneither enabled nor advertised in the capability document.\n100\t\n101\t`bead-rs` still never invokes Git. Automatic flush publishes into the working\n102\ttree; committing remains entirely the caller's business. The plan's standing\n103\trejection of automatic Git publication is unaffected.\n104\t\n105\t## Rationale\n106\t\n107\tThe property that motivates automatic flush is *the durable checkpoint is\n108\tnever silently behind the database*. Coalescing schemes — flush every N\n109\tmutations, flush after T seconds, flush at process exit — reduce cost by\n110\treintroducing exactly the window the change exists to close, and they make the\n111\tgap nondeterministic instead of merely present. If the guarantee is worth\n112\thaving it must be per-mutation.\n113\t\n114\tPer-mutation flushing is affordable only if a flush is proportional to the\n115\tdelta. Section 6.1.1 already designs for this: content-addressed objects\n116\treused byte-for-byte, issue shards split by bead-ID prefix, and audit events\n117\tsealed into append-only tail objects specifically so \"a frequently updated\n118\tbead [does not] rewrite its entire history-bearing issue shard.\" Under that\n119\tdesign a single mutation rewrites one issue shard, appends one event tail\n120\tobject, and publishes a new manifest and pointer. The\n125\tprerequisites are not new scope invented to justify delay: items 1 and 2 above\n126\tare the implementation diverging from section 6.1.1 and 6.2 as already\n127\twritten, and item 3 is a stated invariant that is not upheld. They are\n128\tdefects, and each is independently worth fixing whether or not the flush\n129\tdefault ever changes. What this ADR adds is that automatic flush *multiplies*\n130\tall three by the mutation rate, which promotes them from latent to blocking.\n131\t\n132\tExplicit flush was never valuable in itself. It was the conservative default\n133\tfor a publication step whose cost and correctness were not yet bounded. Once\n134\tthey are, the deliberate-publication argument no longer outweighs a fleet\n135\tlosing work to a missed command.\n136\t\n137\t## Consequences\n138\t\n139\t### Benefits\n140\t\n141\t- A clone, a restore, and a `doctor` run reflect the last mutation rather than\n142\t  the last remembered flush. Operators who ran read-modify\n163\t  loops expecting a quiet tree will see churn, and Git status becomes noisy\n164\t  between commits.\n165\t- It reverses a rule stated in the README, root help, man pages, and the\n166\t  surrounding environment's agent instructions. All of them become wrong on\n167\t  the day the default flips and must change in the same release.\n168\t\n169\t### Alternatives Considered\n170\t\n171\t- **Flush per mutation on the current monolithic path**: rejected. It is the\n172\t  straightforward reading of the request and it is the trap — quadratic bytes\n173\t  written, one leaked full-size object per mutation, and linear-in-workspace\n174\t  latency on every command.\n175\t- **Coalesced flush (every N mutations or T seconds)**: rejected as the\n176\t  default. It preserves a silent staleness window, which is the defect being\n177\t  fixed, and replaces a deterministic gap with a timing-dependent one. It\n178\t  remains a legitimate opt-in for very large workspaces once the automatic\n179\t  path exists.\n180\t- **Flush at process exit**: rejected. Flushing\n190\t  and publishing history are different decisions with different blast radii.\n191\t\n192\t## Implementation\n193\t\n194\tTracked as **R026** in section 12 of the plan, with the normative contract in\n195\tsection 6.2.1. The public `create_issue`\n   (`src/service/issues.rs:14`) writes no audit event — only the unused\n   `create_issue_internal` does — and `dependencies.rs`, `external_refs.rs`,\n   and `data.rs` contain no event inserts at all. For a\nGit-tracked directory that is a repository-size incident, not a slow command —\nthis project's own environment has already absorbed one 817 MB history from\ncommitting large generated artifacts.\n\n## Decision\n\nAdopt **automatic flush on successful mutation as the default behavior**, with\n`--no-auto-flush` and a workspace configuration key as escape hatches, and\n`bead sync flush-only` retained as an explicit idempotent operation.\n\nGate activation on the checkpoint publication path becoming **incremental**.\nAutomatic flush ships only when a flush writes work proportional to the change\nrather than to the workspace. Automatic flush publishes into the working\ntree; committing remains entirely the caller's business. The plan's standing\nrejection of automatic Git publication is unaffected.\n\n## Rationale\n\nThe property that motivates automatic flush is *the durable checkpoint is\nnever silently behind the database*. Coalescing schemes — flush every N\nmutations, flush after T seconds, flush at process exit — reduce cost by\nreintroducing exactly the window the change exists to close, and they make the\ngap nondeterministic instead of merely present. If the guarantee is worth\nhaving it must be per-mutation.\n\nPer-mutation flushing is affordable only if a flush is proportional to the\ndelta. The architecture that makes\nautomatic flush viable is therefore already specified — it is simply not the\none the code takes today.\n\nSequencing the decision this way keeps two things from being confused. The\nprerequisites are not new scope invented to justify delay: items 1 and 2 above\nare the implementation diverging from section 6.1.1 and 6.2 as already\nwritten, and item 3 is a stated invariant that is not upheld. They are\ndefects, and each is independently worth fixing whether or not the flush\ndefault ever changes. What this ADR adds is that automatic flush *multiplies*\nall three by the mutation rate, which promotes them from latent to blocking.\n\nExplicit flush was never valuable in itself. It was the conservative default\nfor a publication step whose cost and correctness were not yet bounded. Once\nthey are, the deliberate-publication argument no longer outweighs a fleet\nlosing work to a missed command.\n\n## Consequences\n\n### Benefits\n\n- A clone, a restore, and a `doctor` run reflect the last mutation rather than\n  the last remembered flush. The command contract must define that\n  split outcome rather than leave it to each call site.\n- Concurrent workers newly contend on checkpoint publication, not just on\n  SQLite. Operators who ran read-modify\n  loops expecting a quiet tree will see churn, and Git status becomes noisy\n  between commits.\n- It reverses a rule stated in the README, root help, man pages, and the\n  surrounding environment's agent instructions. All of them become wrong on\n  the day the default flips and must change in the same release.\n\n### Alternatives Considered\n\n- **Flush per mutation on the current monolithic path**: rejected. It is the\n  straightforward reading of the request and it is the trap — quadratic bytes\n  written, one leaked full-size object per mutation, and linear-in-workspace\n  latency on every command.\n- **Coalesced flush (every N mutations or T seconds)**: rejected as the\n  default. It preserves a silent staleness window, which is the defect being\n  fixed, and replaces a deterministic gap with a timing-dependent one. It\n  remains a legitimate opt-in for very large workspaces once the automatic\n  path exists.\n- **Flush at process exit**: rejected. A crashed or `SIGKILL`ed worker is\n  precisely the case that loses work, and `bead-rs` has no supervising\n  process to fall back on.\n- **A background flushing daemon**: rejected. It is the status\n  quo, it has already failed in practice, and documentation cannot make a\n  missed command observable to the worker that missed it.\n- **Automatic Git commit after flush**: remains rejected, unchanged. Flushing\n  and publishing history are different decisions with different blast radii.\n\n## Implementation\n\nTracked as **R026** in section 12 of the plan, with the normative contract in\nsection 6.2.1. Four prerequisites (P1-P4) must pass before the default flips:\n\n- **P1** — content-address the monolithic root and reuse identical objects.\n- **P2** — apply pointer-declared tombstones; stop listing `current.json` as\n  deleted; bound the retained object set to the generations the pointer and\n  `previous.json` reference.\n- **P3** — emit an audit event for every committed semantic mutation, so the\n  event sequence is a sound dirtiness signal.\n- **P4** — make sharded mode reachable and selected by the recorded thresholds\n  so publication cost tracks the delta.\n\nThen the automatic path itself: a single post-commit publication chokepoint,\ndefined split-failure semantics and exit code, publication locking, the\n`--no-auto-flush` flag and `checkpoint.auto_flush` configuration key, an\n`auto_flush` field in the capability document, and the documentation reversal\nacross README, root help, man pages, and `AGENTS.md`.\n\nThis is a one-time contract change followed by ongoing maintenance of the\nincremental publication path.\n\n## Related\n\n- Plan section 6.1.1 — adaptive sharded checkpoint set (the incremental design\n  this ADR depends on)\n- Plan section 6.2 and new section 6.2.1 — flush algorithm and the automatic\n  flush contract\n- Plan section 12, R026 — automatic checkpoint flush on mutation\n- Plan section 13 — release gate for R026\n- Plan section 3.5.10 — rapid-fire lifecycle capacity benchmarks, which bound\n  the acceptable per-mutation publication cost\n- `research/specs/checkpoint-set-v1.md` — specification-blocked; P1, P2, and\n  P4 are constrained by it\n\n## Supersedes\n\nNone. Class-closing contract test: every mutating command advances the live event\n//! sequence.\n//!\n//! The defect class: a mutating command ships without appending an audit event,\n//! so the live event sequence stops being a sound dirtiness signal. A checkpoint\n//! flush then reads the workspace as clean even though semantic state moved\n//! (plan 6.2.1 P3; ADR-003). Four instances of this class were fixed one at a\n//! time -- the public create path (beadrs-23fea176), dependency mutations\n//!
